utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Good morning to everybody in and around the courtroom. Mr. Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Good morning to everyone in and around the courtroom. This is case number IT-04-81-T, the Prosecutor versus Momcilo Perisic. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much. Could we have appearances for the day, starting with the Prosecution, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Good morning to everybody in and around the courtroom. Carmela Javier and Barney Thomas for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much. And for the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Good morning to all. Boris Zorko, Chad Mair, Alex Fielding, and Gregor Guy-Smith on behalf of the Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much, Mr. Guy-Smith. Good morning, Mr. Vuksic, just to remind you, and I know you know this already, but you have to be reminded that you are still bound by the declaration you made at the beginning of your testimony to tell the truth, the whole truth, and nothing else but the truth.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much, Mr. Vuksic. Yes, Mr. Guy-Smith.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: With regard to your duties, were you involved in arranging, what I would call, meetings or shows, for example, an air show, between your country and your army and other countries and their armies?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VUKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, I was. For the sake of clarity, may I add that one of the tasks of the department that I headed was to deal with organisational matters and protocol and the contacts we had within the framework of international military co-operation. Therefore, the organisation of any kind of event or any kind of meeting meant that certain organisational measures had to be taken and to observe proper protocol as was part of international practice.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: In that regard, in terms of the context that you had within the framework of international military co-operation, were you involved in setting up any air shows with any foreign governments or foreign military?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Question asked and answered. That's the way you began.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Could you --

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You are welcome.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Could you be more specific with regard to the foreign governments and foreign military that you set up such meetings as an air show with, and by that I mean identify who they were?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VUKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, as far as I can remember, there were two air shows.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: When was the first air show?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VUKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In 1976 -- or, rather, 1996. I am sorry, that was a mistake. I misspoke. And the second one was 1997. Both were held at the military airport in Batajnica.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Can you tell us who was involved, what countries were involved in those air shows?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VUKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Aircraft from Russia, Greece.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Anyone else, or is that the extent of it?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VUKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: And France. France.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Any other countries?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VUKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think there were other countries too, but I cannot recall right now. The most important presence there was the air force of the Republic of France.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And when you say "the most important presence was the air force of the Republic of France," why was that the most important presence?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VUKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I think it is primarily due to the time when the events were being held, the time when my country, the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, and its army were not fully breathing yet, if I can put it that way. The situation had not become normal again yet, and we were not in a position to establish normal military relations within the framework of overall bilateral relations with individual countries. France was still a member of the Contact Group. The Contact Group was discussing important issues, some related to Yugoslavia as well. France took part from the very outset with parts of its armed forces in all the missions and all the forces that were in the territory of Yugoslavia. Over a long period of time - I cannot be more specific - was the country that had the largest presence within UNPROFOR. France sent, to UNPROFOR, about 7.000 men, 7.000 soldiers and members of the armed force of France. Three French generals were commanders of UNPROFOR for over three years. The first commander for -- of UNPROFOR for Bosnia-Herzegovina, that is to say, the most sensitive and most tragic area, was French General Morillon, and so on and so forth. France was very active politically, and our feeling as far as France was concerned was that France was a traditional friend and ally, in view of everything that had happened during the First World War.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Thank you for that response, Mr. Vuksic. I now am going to remain in the area of the air but move into a slightly different topic. We previously have discussed the issue of violation of air-space, and that was with regard to violation of air-space by UNPROFOR. I'd now like to discuss with you whether or not you recall whether or not there was any discussions concerning air-space violation by the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia in 1994 that you were a part of?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VUKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you allow me, Mr. Guy-Smith, I would just like to correct what you said. Let us be more specific, if possible; sometimes that is simply not possible because of my faint recollections. This has to do with violations of the no-fly zone over Bosnia-Herzegovina, later on Croatia as well. After the Dayton Agreement, it also had to do with the air-space above Eastern Slavonia, Western Slavonia, Baranja, as it was called at the time. --

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. Vuksic, we may well get to that particular issue, but right now I'm confining the question to the period of time of 1994. We'll have an opportunity to discuss other years, but right now I'd like you to confine your answer to 1994, if you would be so kind.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VUKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I understand and thank you. What I was trying to say was that that was a topical issue from the very outset. There were quite a few discussions as to who was violating the no-fly zone and how in Bosnia-Herzegovina in 1994 as well and that I took part in those discussions.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Thank you. Could we please have brought up on the screen 65 ter 522D.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Which would be tab 12 in your binder, Mr. Vuksic. And if you would be so kind to take a look at this particular document. And after you've had a chance to review it, could you please indicate that you've had a chance to review the document.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VUKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have just familiarised myself with this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: This document is dated the 29th of October, 1994, and it is entitled: "Report on results of investigation to allegations of violations of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia air-space on 19 through 20 October 1994 and measures taken." Were you involved with regard to any investigations concerning violations of air-space on those dates?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VUKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In a classical sense, I could not have been involved in the investigation that involved a technical and technological process, that is to say, the professional side of the problem. However, it was my duty to convey to the appropriate organs the suspicions of the representatives of international organisations, UNPROFOR specifically, namely, that aircraft of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia had violated the air-space of Bosnia-Herzegovina thereby violating the ban; or that we, the Army of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, had information that aircraft of the international forces that were enforcing the no-fly zone had violated the air-space of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia; or that this was done by one of the warring parties in Bosnia-Herzegovina. So it is in that sense that the document that was signed by General Perisic was quite naturally written inter alia on the basis of what I had done in the course of my own duties, that is to say, on the basis of my own reporting or the reporting of my department, or, rather, the department that I headed and that was involved in dealing with that problem.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: With regard to the document in front of you, looking at paragraph number 1, the first entry indicates that: "None of the VJ Yugoslav Army helicopters was in the air at the given time and in the given sector." Is that information that you were aware of?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VUKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I could not have known about that because, as I already said, I did not take part in the technological part of that process of establishing the truth. That was not within the scope of my duty.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Apart from the, as you put it, the technological part of the investigation, did you receive information from anyone concerning this investigation with regard to the technological findings that were made such that you were in a position to report back to your counter-parts with regard to the findings?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VUKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You have worded this question so very nicely and therefore it is easier for me to answer the question. Yes, I did get answers to the documents that I sent and in which I had stated that international factors believe that aircraft of the Army of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia had violated the no-fly zone in Bosnia-Herzegovina. I conveyed the information I received to the representatives of the forces and missions that were in contact with me. It wasn't all that rarely, so I cannot remember any specific cases, and no specific case is of particular relevance now. However, may I repeat that the Chief of General Staff had decided that a document should be written up that he would sign, and that very fact meant that the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, or rather, the Army of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia wanted to do its very best to avoid such things ever happening. If there were any suspicions voiced, then they wanted to respond to them with proper argumentation.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Understanding that you cannot remember at this time any specific cases, I'm going to move to the second part of this document and ask you whether or not you recall as to the measures that were decided to be instituted with regard to air-space violations and whether or not you conveyed those measures to your counter-parts. And I'm referring you to paragraph number 2 in which a number of measures are set forth. The following measures -- it states: "The following measures were taken to prevent uncontrolled flights across the FRY-RS border. In addition to the existing surveillance system, an order has been issued to increase radar observation by engaging one company and two platoons, Vojin, and to increase visual observation by VJ border units. A reminder was issued that VRS helicopters have been prohibited from flying in the FRY territory, apart from humanitarian purposes with prior permission." Are those matters that you became aware of after the investigation occurred in terms of the kinds of remedies that were being sought by General Perisic to cope with this problem?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VUKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Thank you. Furthermore, were you made aware of some of the difficulties that would -- were envisioned as potentially existing, and by that I mean referring to paragraph 3 of this document, General Perisic states: "Despite the measures that have been applied, we would like to point out that complete control of air-space is not possible at an altitude below 100 metres and in a rugged terrain. Possibility for surveillance is considerably reduced in mountainous areas." Is that something you became privy to after the investigation as a cautionary note with regard to the measures that could be taken and instituted by FRY pursuant to the direction of General Perisic?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VUKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I knew that as a soldier too within the framework of my general knowledge of the armed forces. I knew that if aircraft flew at low altitudes, they would fly below the radar, as we say, so this is an expression. And General Perisic is actually cautioning about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And finally with regard to a report of General Perisic, paragraph 4, indicating measures to be taken: "Aircraft that have flown into the FRY without permission shall be kept. If these measures are not respected, the anti-aircraft defence system shall be activated and measures under the rules for preventing air-space violations of the FRY territory." Were you made privy to those particular determinations by General Perisic as to what would occur in the event that there were air-space violations into the territory of FRY?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VUKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I knew of such measures, that they could and should be taken.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VUKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were --

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I would move this document's admission.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You've read the entire document into the record, Mr. Guy-Smith.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: No, I haven't, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Well, virtually.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Well, but - I understand that - but I have not read the entire document into the record.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Well, you know, I'm just trying to remind you of the guide-lines that if you are going to tender a document, you don't have to read through it; but if you are going to read through it, then there is no need to do that, we have that guide-line.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I appreciate that, Your Honour. I understand that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: And you have read virtually 75 per cent of this document into the record.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I haven't gone through a quantitative analysis of how much of the document I've read line by line. I seek to tender the document into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: But I'm just warning you for the future.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you. The document is admitted into evidence. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, this document shall be assigned Exhibit D366. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I'd like to stay on the subject for a moment, if we could, of air-space issues. And turn your attention to 1995. And I request that you take a look at tab 24 in your binder, which is 65 ter 1162D.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VUKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'll just familiarise myself with this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Are you the author of this document, sir?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VUKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I decided to have it written up, and I signed it.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I seek its admission.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The document is admitted into evidence. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, this document shall be assigned Exhibit D367. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Excuse me, if I might. Returning to -- it's page 9, line 11. I'm informed that the answer that was given by the witness was "I knew of such measures, that they could" -- sorry. That the answer he gave was: "That they could and should be taken" and were taken. And the answer, as given, excludes the last part of that: "And were taken." And I'm now getting a confirmatory nod by Mr. Lukic who has also joined us, that that is what the witness said with regard to that answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Do you confirm that, Mr. Vuksic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I'm not certain what exactly this is about. If what we are talking about are the measures mentioned by General Perisic in his document, in that case we should all proceed with great caution. What that would mean is the airplanes of the UN peacekeeping forces that were actually violating the air-space were held up at one point, or that the anti-aircraft defence systems were set in motion --

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Mr. Vuksic --

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VUKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- which is a delicate issue as far as I know.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... it may well be a delicate issue, and I do hate to interrupt you, but the Judge asked you a very specific question and I think you owe him the courtesy of answering the question that was asked, which is: Do you confirm that your answer included that those measures were taken, as you are sitting here?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VUKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. No.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you. With regard to the last exhibit that we just looked at, you indicated there was an attachment to that exhibit, to that letter, which was the report of the co-chairman. And I'd like to have you go to your binder, if you might, and take a look at tab number 27, which is P2485. If you could take a look at the document. And my question is: Is this the document that you appended to the letter that you wrote on the 17th of May, 1995, the exhibit that we just referred to?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VUKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Thank you. It can be taken off the screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I'd like to direct your attention to --

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honours, I couldn't get my hands on the hard copy of that document. I was waiting for the English to appear on the screen because we had two B/C/S copies. I just want to view that document briefly before ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Just before the two B/C/S copies came onto the screen, the English one disappeared. It was hardly a second on the screen. If it can be brought back.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: Thank you, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: If it's of any assistance, Mr. Thomas, I have a hard copy here in English.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: It's fine, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Are we good?

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I'd like to turn our attention, if we could, to September of 1995. I'd like to ask you if you recall there being any air-strikes during that period of time which were the subject matter of conversations between you and your counter-parts in international organisations and foreign military attachés?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VUKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What you have in mind is probably the NATO air-strikes targeting the positions and facilities belonging to the VRS, which went on for quite sometime and spread to early September. In that case, the answer is yes, I was in a position to raise this with a number of different persons, specifically including international military representatives.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And what was the -- if you could expand a bit here, sir, what was the cause of concern with regard to these air-strikes?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VUKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The NATO air-strikes targeting the positions and facilities of the VRS were an ultimate measure taken by international players, and here I mean the UN along with everyone else, in a bid to force the hand of the political and military leadership of Republika Srpska and get them to behave in a certain way or to correct their behaviour as it had been up to that point, especially in terms of releasing hostages taken from the ranks of the UN peacekeeping forces, persons which they had previously arrested in response to NATO's air-strikes. If you so require, sir, I can tell you what else they were asked to do.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: That's fine. Thank you. With regard to what you've stated thus far, were you made privy at any time to the concerns raised by the permanent representative of the Russian Federation Ambassador Lavrov concerning these air-strikes, and specifically the air-strike on the Stolce communications tower?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VUKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, given the nature of my official capacity, it was my duty, to the extent that I could, to follow what was going on on the political plane. I was well aware of Russia's different views and position, generally speaking, regarding the behaviour of Republika Srpska, both in a political and in a military sense. Their positions differed to some extent from those represented by their partners in the Contact Group and other international bodies. I also discussed this with their own military envoy.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: With regard to the issue of the air-strike on Stolce tower, were you made privy to the position taken in this regard, that the Stolce communication tower was outside of a permissible area for NATO air-strike and that NATO had embarked upon a policy of disproportionate and wide-ranging air-strikes without any authority? Were you made aware of that?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I have a problem, Mr. Guy-Smith. You virtually have swapped positions with the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Does that mean I get to sit down?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: No, that means you are -- you are testifying, and, you know --

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I'm asking whether he was made privy to a position. He was made privy to a position, yes or no --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: But that's -- that's --

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: But that's not the thrust of the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The point --

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Excuse me, Your Honour, let me finish.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: No, but you are interrupting me when I'm speaking. Your question should be, What were you -- what do you know about what happened? You know --

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Excuse me, Your Honour, if I might. I'm not testifying. And the point here is not a point with regard to necessarily what Ambassador Lavrov said but, rather, if armed with this information, he did anything. Which is specifically a different issue. If Ambassador Lavrov said, for example, that he felt something was incorrect, that he, he, Ambassador Lavrov, had difficulties with what was being done and that information was communicated, he was privy to that information and he used that information with regard to his contacts with UN organisations or his contacts with military attachés, that is a point. Now that is something I can ask him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The point --

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And that is the thrust of the question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The point is you got to ask this witness, if you are not to lead him, what interaction he had with Lavrov, what Lavrov told him, and what he did about it. Not for you to --

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: He may not have been -- he may not have had any interaction with --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ... if he hasn't had any interaction what Lavrov, then he can't tell you anything that he did about what Lavrov did.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Oh, but of course he can. And it happens all the time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: But he can tell you. He can --

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: But excuse me, Your Honour. If I -- if I say, for example, to you --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] I am a going to rule on this one, okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers]... well, it's conceptually -- conceptually -- conceptually it's foreclosing -- it's foreclosing an area of an examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I'm not foreclosing an area of examination.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for the president, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You can ask this witness if he had any interaction with Lavrov. If he didn't have any interaction with Lavrov, if he has any information about what Lavrov might have done, and, if so, what he did with it. But it has got to be this witness who testifies, otherwise there's no point in calling witnesses if we are going to be testifying, ourselves, from the bar.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Well, I understand the point you're taking. I happen to disagree with it, but --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: That's fine, but that's the point --

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers]... that's neither here nor there for purposes of where we are right now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Right. Then do what I'm asking you to do then.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Did you have any interaction with Ambassador Lavrov, the permanent representative of the Russian Federation?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VUKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. No direct interaction.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Did you have any indirect interaction with Ambassador Lavrov, the permanent representative of the Russian Federation?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VUKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If we can apply that to the established practice, for example --

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Excuse me, sir, stop there. You say the "established practice," could you please explain to the Chamber what the established practice was?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VUKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sure. There were official policies which provided a certain framework, and the country set out certain official policies. Measures are taken within that framework. This implies that certain positions are taken and made official by representatives of that country. These positions are then interpreted and verified by all other officials of the country at what is perhaps a lower level, but this must always be in line with the positions received from the appropriate authorities in their own country.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Understanding what you've just said, did you in your capacity receive any information about what Ambassador Lavrov might have done?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VUKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: What information did you -- excuse me, Mr. Vuksic. I want to make sure that we do not offend. What information did you receive as to what Ambassador Lavrov might have done?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VUKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I received oral information conveyed to me by Russia's military envoy, General Viktor Dimitrijevic - I can't remember his third name - which is perfectly common with Russians and might in fact be of some importance.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And you indicated that you received oral information which indicates -- and I understand that you are referring to oral information as opposed to written information. With regard to the oral information that you received from General Viktor Dimitrijevic, what factual oral information did you receive from him with regard to what Ambassador Lavrov might have done?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VUKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: General Dimitrijevic asked me whether I knew about the declaration and the measures take been by their official representative to the UN, Ambassador Lavrov. I said that I knew about that but probably not sufficiently. I said I would be grateful to him if he were to tell me more about that. General Dimitrijevic, understandably, expressed his satisfaction at being given an opportunity to interpret to me the meaning and purpose of Mr. Lavrov's declaration or statement. Over the course of the exchange, what I found out from him comes down to more or less what is said here. What he shared with me was meant to convince me that Russia was pursuing a principled policy in this case and that it would remain adamant in terms of trying to correct some errors that were occurring vis-à-vis the Serb side, conditionally speaking. I was not personally entirely convinced at all times.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I do hate to interrupt you. You've said "the Serb side, conditionally speaking," I'm not sure what you mean when you use the term "conditionally speaking." If you could clarify that term, when you say "the Serb side, conditionally speaking," I'd appreciate it.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VUKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I'm used to being misunderstood when I speak like that. That kind of misunderstanding has been a frequent occurrence ever since the outbreak of the crisis in the former Yugoslavia, and it still goes on. There were some players who tried to define who the parties were to this crisis, and they found different expressions for this. When the Russians talked about the Serb side, they meant Serbian people as found throughout the territory of the former Yugoslavia, and their right to entertain mutual relations and in a way live side by side. I understand that then, as now, some people might find it difficult to understand. It also meant, as far as policies were concerned, as well as possible errors, that the country that was wronged in some ways at the time was the country that had the majority of Serbs living in it, which, at the time, was the FRY. But that also applied to those living in Bosnia-Herzegovina and in Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: If I might interject. You indicated in your response that over the course of the -- this is at page 17, line 25, continuing to page 18, line 1: "Over the course of the exchange, what I found out from him comes down to more or less what is said here." When you are referring to what is said here, what are you alluding to there, "what is said here"? I don't know what you are alluding to there.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VUKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is said, and then the Stolice radio relay station is mentioned. This is near Tuzla in Bosnia-Herzegovina. This was an important hub in the signals and command system of the VRS. The Muslim military units did their best to destroy this radio relay hub and leave it unable to operate. This was a particularly delicate issue which drew a lot of attention and interest. The representatives of certain NATO countries as well as the representatives of certain international organisations tried to phrase this cautiously in order to say they were not fully in the clear as to what was going on in Bosnia-Herzegovina and whether NATO's air force was in fact operating in keeping with the UN mandate and conventions. Specifically, the military advisors in the Belgrade UN office were people that I used to meet on a regular basis, or at least a frequent one. They couch this in very cautious terms, but their point was clear; they said they did not understand this either.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VUKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There would always be two or three advisors in that office.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Now, I'm going to jump ahead in time, but we will be spending a considerable period of time on this particular issue. But I'm jumping ahead in time because of the manner in which this particular document is comprised. And there's information in this document that I'd like to discuss with you to see whether or not you have an understanding of this or not. Directing your attention to the 1st of September, 1995, were you involved in any meetings that day with General Mladic and others concerning issues such as the French pilots?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VUKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not attend the meeting with General Mladic that September. I did meet him, however, several days before that meeting and perhaps also several days after.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: With regard to the meeting on the 1st of September, to your knowledge were there any air-strikes that day by NATO?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VUKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were air-strikes. I can't say whether on that very day; nevertheless, the air-strikes were quite frequent at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: As a result of the meetings that were had with General Mladic -- let me back up there. Do you know who was involved in the meetings with General Mladic?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VUKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What I knew is on that day General Perisic would be on his way --

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Excuse me, I'm only asking you for the participants in the meeting, not for what occurred at this point in time.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VUKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I apologise. Yes, I know who the participants were.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Who were they?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VUKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: One of the negotiating sides was represented by General Janvier who, at the time, was commander of the UN peacekeeping forces. He was also the person who initiated this meeting. His counter-part on the other side was General Mladic, commander of the General Staff of the VRS. How did this meeting come about? The meeting was brokered, to put it that way, by General Perisic.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Before we get involved in the meeting, after the meeting on the 1st, did you become aware of what the various sides' positions were with regard to what needed to be done by both General Mladic's side as well as Janvier's side as it related to further air-strikes. Or put in other terms: Were conditions set forth by the respective parties concerning these negotiations?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VUKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I had very little direct knowledge about the substance of the actual conversation at that meeting. Nevertheless, I understood the gist of what the whole thing was about. I had previously debated some of the same problems with people before that meeting as well as after. That notwithstanding, I had the good or bad luck, depending on how you look at it, to have a chance to familiarise myself with a report from that meeting. It wasn't before then that I realised that this had indeed been a very dramatic and significant meeting. Significant why? Because of the topics that were raised and debated and the problems that were raised.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: With regard to the topics --

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VUKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Why was it --

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: With regard to the topics that were raised, are you in a position to assist us in that regard as to the topics that were raised and discussed?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VUKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I think that there were three or four issues on the agenda -- or, rather, requests posed by General Janvier which were interpreted by General Mladic as an ultimatum. The first one was --

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Thank you, I was going to ask you specifically and what were those requests?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VUKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was just about to tell you that. If my answers are somewhat too long, this is not because I wish to do that or because I enjoy reminiscing about these events, but I'm rather afraid that the knowledge that we have about this difficult time differs among different people --

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Mr. Vuksic --

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VUKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Maybe I'm not doing it in a very skillful way. If that is the case, I do apologise.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: MR. Vuksic, I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you for that warning, Mr. Vuksic. Could you now get to the answer. We will remember that warning you've given us.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The first condition or request put forward was for the heavy weaponry deployed around Sarajevo be moved at -- 20 kilometres away from Sarajevo. That was a request that had been repeated continuously, but which the warring parties did not want to implement. As far as I know, the VRS for the most part was reluctant to do that, but the same applied to the Muslim army as well. The second request was not to attack the remaining protected areas, UN protected areas. And by that I mean that the VRS had already entered Srebrenica and Zepa. The third request, as far as I can remember, was to allow free access or free passage to humanitarian and other convoys that were delivering supplies to Sarajevo and the areas populated by refugees and who needed this relief badly.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Were there any other issues on the agenda that you can recall?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: In fact, you said there were four items, Mr. Vuksic; you've given us three.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I said three or four. I cannot remember exactly at the moment. There may have been even more than that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VUKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course, I have to say this because it's very important in the context: The NATO air-strikes and bombing would have been suspended. But when I said earlier whether it was on that date that air-strikes took place, I had in mind the fact that for that specific occasion General Janvier ordered the air-strikes to stop, but I think that he extended this period to 72 hours, if I remember correctly.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Do you recall what happened after the 72-hour remit in air-strikes terminated? Did the air-strikes cease from that time? Did they start up again?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VUKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe that the outcome of the meeting was not such that resulted in the termination of NATO air-strikes. And the bombing continued, as far as I am aware.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I would seek admission of this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: We've lost it from our screen. What was its 65 ter number?

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] 65 ter 2109D.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: 2109D. May the document please be admitted into evidence and be given an exhibit number. I don't remember seeing this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: Your Honour, it's not appeared on the screen because I think my learned friend, through oversight, never asked for to be put up there. But I wonder if we could just have it on the screen before it's admitted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Could we have it, because I'm seeing this 65 ter 2109D for the first time.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I thought I put it up on the screen. My apologies, Mr. Thomas. My apologies to Chamber.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, it's definitely coming for the first time. Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: That's fine, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you. The document is admitted into evidence. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, this document shall be assigned Exhibit D368. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Before we go any further, I need to go back for a moment. On page 20, beginning at line 18, I asked you the following question and you gave me the following answer: "Excuse me, I'm only asking you for the participants in the meeting, not for what occurred at this point in time." And your answer is: "I apologise. Yes, I know who the participants were." My next question to you was: "Who were they?" And your answer was: "One of the negotiating sides was represented by General" -- and as the transcript read there at the present it says General G, "who at the time was the commander of the peacekeeping forces. He was also the side ... was General Mladic, commander of the General Staff of the VRS." And then what I have on the transcript is: "... how ... way, by General Perisic?" Now, I'd like to get a bit of clarification here, just in case something has been missed, which is: With regard to this meeting, you have mentioned a number of names, and if you could tell us who was the commander of the peacekeeping forces at that meeting, his name?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VUKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think I already said that that was General Janvier. I mentioned his name several times. And if you allow me in that respect --

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Vuksic. There's no question pending at this time. I need to get a clarification for this particular answer. With regard to your answer, you have indicated that General Perisic was involved. Could you please explain to us what General Perisic's involvement was with regard to the meeting between Janvier and Mladic?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VUKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have to say, again, that I should be allowed to say at least a few sentences in order for us to comprehend this issue as a whole.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Mr. Vuksic, I appreciate what you believe should be done. There's certain information that we need to get. After we get that information, a determination will be made with regard to whether or not further discussion from you is necessary. So, once again, sir, with regard to the meeting between General Janvier and General Mladic, what was General Perisic's involvement, if you know?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VUKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The role of General Perisic was known for quite some time, and it involved making every effort on our part to set up a meeting between international representatives who were asking for it and General Mladic. And they wanted to meet General Mladic specifically. We tried to implement that in the shortest possible time and in the simplest way. We also wanted to assist in approximating views during such meetings and in finding solutions, and by providing assistance meant that we should do everything in our power to achieve that.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Your Honour, we are going to be moving into a new topic. I note the time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much. We'll take a break and come back at quarter to 11.00. Court adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Guy-Smith.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Mr. Vuksic, if you could turn to tab 23 in your binder.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: That would be 65 ter 1161D, Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And if you could take a moment and look at the document and indicate when you've reviewed the document, please.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VUKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm familiar with this document. It's very short. I signed it, and I know what the purpose was.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay. Could you identify for us, if possible, who Colonel Pug is? Which is a name in the document.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VUKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Colonel Pug was an officer in the escort of General de Lapresle, the previous commander of the UN peacekeeping forces; and now he was a special envoy of the President of the Republic of France Mr. Chirac.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And could you tell us what the purpose of asking permission to approve the crossing to Republika Srpska was for?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VUKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is difficult for me to give you a short answer, but I'll do my best. For quite some time the relations between the VJ and the minister of the interior were deteriorating. But, please, what I just said, take with a certain reserve because I don't have enough time to explain such a complex problem. I can only add something that in my view is truthful, and I leave it to everyone else to construe it or abuse it in any way they wish. These relations depended on the will of Slobodan Milosevic. From the very outset of the Yugoslav crisis, when he became a prominent figure, favoured the police.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I am sorry, Mr. Vuksic, I've asked you a very specific question and I understand that your answer can't be short, but if you could first pay attention to the question asked and then thereafter we'll make a determination what further explanation is needed. And my question to you was: And could you tell us what the purpose of asking permission to approve the crossing to Republika Srpska was for?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VUKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Under normal circumstances, each organ takes care of their duties. I would like to say that the situation and the relations in the then-Yugoslavia and the region were not normal at the time. We wanted to normalise those situations and relations, and we wanted that everyone do their respective job properly. In order to thwart any misunderstandings, we informed the competent authorities within the Ministry of the Interior, and in this particular case it was the police general Pusovic [phoen]. We informed him about the fact that a representative of the UN peacekeeping forces was asking to go to Republika Srpska and that we were going to escort him at a certain time across the so-called border.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: To your knowledge, was this achieve? And by that, was the representative of the UN peacekeeping forces allowed to go across the border -- I'm sorry, allowed to go, as you put it, the so-called border?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VUKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I was informed about that by Colonel Vasiljevic and Major Davidovic who were officers on duty in the administration that I headed. I'm sorry, it says here Colonel Vasiljevic and Major Vasiljevic [as interpreted], but it should be the other way around. It's Major Vasiljevic and Colonel Davidovic. And in that connection, if you allow me, in the previous session I wanted to ask a question whether the way I'm talking is acceptable to the interpreters. Nobody has warned me about the pace that I speak.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I trust your pace is all right, otherwise we would hear from the interpreters; they would intervene. They often intervene with me, Mr. Vuksic, and tell me that I'm doing something which could be improved upon, so I'm sure you're doing just right. I thank you for your responses.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And I would move to the admission of that document, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The document is admitted into evidence. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours. This document shall be assigned Exhibit D369. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Now, I'd like to discuss another document with you in situations -- and that would be your tab 4, which is P2708.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I'm hearing that I perhaps should be in private session. I'm hearing quite strongly that I should be in private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: May the Chamber please move into private session.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are in private session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar. Yes, Mr. Lukic -- Mr. Guy-Smith, I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I take that as a compliment; I don't know whether Mr. Lukic does. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] ... take it as a slip of tongue. To Mr. Saxon, I've done the same thing to him.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: First of all, if you could just take a look at the very first page of that document and note the date which is the -- that I have here is 27/10/1995. And with regard to the permission that you had sought which was in the previous document discussed, that's D369, I'm wondering whether or not if you could tell us, is this -- if you know, is this the meeting that you were seeking passage for General de Lapresle and Colonel Pug? Since the date is the same, that's the reason I'm asking the question.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VUKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, there is no doubt about that. By looking at this document, I have no doubt that the previous letter referred to the crossing of the border by General de Lapresle in order to attend this particular meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you for that response.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: We can take that document off the screen. And if we could go back into open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: May the Chamber please move into open session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are back in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much, Mr. Registrar. Yes, Mr. Guy-Smith.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Do you know an individual by the name of General Gracev [phoen]?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VUKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Who is he?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VUKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the time when I met him, he was the minister of defence of the Russian Federation of Russia.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: To your knowledge, what involvement, if any, did General Gracev have concerning the issue of the French pilots?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VUKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, he was.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And when you say "yes, he was," what was he? And by that I mean, what was his involvement?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VUKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is what I mean by his involvement: Primarily the interest the Russian representatives, and I mean military attachés, expressed, as well as members of the Russian contingent within UNPROFOR. They took an interest in this problem. If you ask me, perhaps a little more than -- again, if you ask me, might be considered normal.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Irrespective of whether or not their interest was normal, above normal, or below normal, what was the interest that they took? And specifically, what was the interest that the minister of defence Gracev took, if you know, with regard to the issue of the French pilots? If you know. If you don't, that's fine.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VUKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the time, based on those conversations, I was able to conclude - I repeat, to conclude - that General Gracev was paying particular attention to this issue. At the time --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Vuksic, we understand that he paid particular attention. I think the thrust of the question is, Was he for the release, or was he for the continued detention of the pilots? Which side was he on? What was his position in this issue? I guess I'm interpreting you correctly, Mr. Guy-Smith?

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I certainly appreciate the assistance, Your Honour, yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The position taken by him and his representatives was to have the pilots released and set free.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And with regard to the position that he took to have the pilots released and set free, did he indicate, if you know, whether or not he was or was not willing to become personally involved in receiving the pilots himself, to having the pilots delivered to him?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VUKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the time, based on those conversations, I was unable to glean that as something that was certain. Nevertheless, one could surmise that the Russian side and probably Minister Gracev as well were quite prepared to take another step. Nevertheless, I was unable to conclude at the time what that step might be and what its meaning might be.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Thank you for that response. I'd like to continue with the issue of the release of the French pilots. Do you by any chance know what their names were? I mean, I've noticed that over the years everybody talks about the release of the French pilots but nobody's ever given them any names. Do you, by any chance, know what their names were?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VUKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Those are names that emerged somewhere in my consciousness and then are gone again. I think one of them was called Major Vasuev [phoen], and I can't remember the other man's name. I'm sure that I will eventually be able to dredge it up from somewhere in my memory.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Were there only two?

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: If I were to --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for counsel, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: If I were to give you the names of Frederic Chiffot and Jose Souvignet, would that refresh your recollection with regard to the names of the two French pilots?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VUKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. And thank you very much for that, Mr. Guy-Smith. Our pronunciation of these names at the time is a different matters; it's very much a matter of our knowledge of the French language or perhaps lack of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I may be taking liberty with my pronunciation as well. And if I am, I take -- I do apologise; I don't mean to offend. I'm wanting more to acknowledge these two gentlemen for a minute. In any event, with regard to the incident that we are referring to in October, do you know whether or not the French pilots were released in October?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VUKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were not released in October 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: How about November, was there any success in November?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VUKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were not released in November 1995 either.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: To your knowledge, what efforts, if any, were made by General Perisic with regard to obtaining the release of the French pilots in the month of November?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VUKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, General Perisic made some serious efforts and did everything in his power to get the pilots released.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Let's move to the month of December, then, shall we. Now, in the month of December, were the French pilots released?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VUKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The pilots you mentioned were eventually released in December 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: With regard to the release of these two gentlemen, what, if any, importance was their release to resolution of the general crisis at the time in the region?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VUKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Their release was exceptionally important. President Jacques Chirac saw their release as a prerequisite for the signing of the Dayton Peace Accords in Paris.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: With what you've just said in mind, are you aware of any meetings that occurred in December, before the release of these two gentlemen, with regard to obtaining their release that involved General Perisic?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VUKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't say what all of the things were that General Perisic did in order to get the pilots released, which eventually happened in December 1995. Mentioning some of these steps would not constitute the entire context. I do, however, know of two particularly important meetings, one of which I personally attended. One thing that is noteworthy in this context is that it was as a result of this meeting that the pilots were released the very next day in Mali Zvornik.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Well, let us talk about this first meeting that you were present at. When was that meeting?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VUKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I remember, it was held on the 11th of December, 1995, at the Batajnica military airport in Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And who were the participants in that meeting as you remember?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VUKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Chief of the joint General Staff of the armed forces of France, General -- you see, his name escapes me right now. Perhaps if you could give me a hand with that. And his --

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: If I were to mention the name of Douin to you, which I may be pronouncing and probably pronouncing incorrectly --

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VUKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, yes. There you go. I'm gradually getting tired. General Jacques Douin, with General Ratko Mladic as his counter-part in these negotiations, accompanied by Generals Gvero and Tolimir. The role of mediator was again played by General Perisic. For that occasion, he order General Velickovic, the then-commander of the air force and anti-aircraft defence, to be present, as well as Colonel-General Dimitrijevic, chief of the security administration of the VJ.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And before General Douin arrived with his group, was it decided whether this was going to be a public meeting or private meeting? Was this an official meeting? How would you characterise the kind of meeting that was being held on the air strip?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VUKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Our side, if I may call it that, and by that I mean General Perisic, wanted to make the occasion as official and as important as possible. General Douin was to receive the military salute, and he was to be welcomed by a military band. The usual honours extended to a high-ranking soldier like him. Being familiar, as I was, with the procedure around the ceremonial aspects, I was quite skeptical about how this would work. I knew General Perisic, and I did not believe that a thing like this might work. I believe that General Douin would have preferred to leave this visit a little more informal and have as little pomp as possible attaching to it, which is what eventually happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Before what happened, when General Douin's plane landed, was there a military band with all of the attendant honours that befit somebody of his stature available to greet him?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VUKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The unit that was supposed to welcome the general was lined up and the band was there. This is standard procedure in most countries when welcoming such a high-ranking military officer. General Douin was able to see this from the plane as he was on his way in. So we were there standing for him and waiting to welcome him and receive him, but he just wouldn't get off the plane.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: May I just interrupt a little bit.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Sure.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You indicated a couple of minutes ago, Mr. Vuksic, that you were beginning to get tired. Are you in a position to carry on, or do you like a break?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, thank you for your concern. It was just a remark in passing, asking for your forgiveness for being temporarily unable to remember a single name, names even of those people I used to know quite well and that I remember with great fondness; as opposed to my previous observation when I try to say that all of these are developments that I did my best to repress and drive out of my mind and memory. Nevertheless, I'm perfectly fit to continue my testimony, and thank you for your concern.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much. Yes, Mr. Guy-Smith.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: You indicated that General Douin would not get off the plane. What, if anything, transpired at that point in time? As I understand it, there's a band ready to strike up the appropriate tunes, General Perisic and others are in attendance waiting for General Douin to get off the plane, and he is not getting off the plane. What happened?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VUKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'll try to keep this as brief as possible. General Perisic got into the plane and told us what to do. We reminded him that we were the hosts and perhaps we could see our guest inside the plane for a minute to see what the problem was. That is what we eventually did. We realised that General Douin was not willing to be welcomed with the usual military honours. We accepted that. The unit and the band were told to leave the scene, and General Douin eventually got off the plane. We exchanged greetings and --

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Let me --

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VUKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- continued with our contacts.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Did General Douin give you any indication at all as to why he was not willing to get off the plane and enjoy the acknowledgement of the band and the official contact?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VUKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the time, there was no time to discuss that on the runway or in the plane itself. Nevertheless, it soon became clear.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: What became clear?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VUKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When -- when, yes, when we sat down in that room where we were to hold our talks, General Douin realised that General Mladic was not there, nor anyone standing in for him. He asked when and if the pilots would be handed over to him. He made it a condition for meeting General Mladic. He even went so far as to say, I refuse to talk with a man suspected of war crimes. This was a very serious remark. We representing the VJ, General Perisic, and the people who were with him exchanged glances, realising that we were facing some difficult moments and hours ahead. We realised the misunderstanding between the two parties was enormous and that General Douin was probably expecting that he would just put in an appearance that the pilots would be delivered to him in shorter order, having previously undergone a medical check, and that he would be leaving the Batajnica air strip and the FRY air-space that same day, that he would soon be on his way back to Paris to inform President Chirac that he had completed his mission.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Where was Mladic?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VUKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mladic was in the room right next to this one.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: If General Douin was in one room and Mladic was in the other room, what was the difficulty that was occurring? Why couldn't they both be in the same room?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VUKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: General Mladic arrived at the Batajnica airport, but I don't know when exactly. It wasn't my place to know when he would be appearing. I was in charge of knowing when General Douin would be arriving though. Having finished our conversation with General Douin, I think it was General Perisic who tried to make the general see what the reality of our situation was and what he would now have to face up to. We tried to tell him that we -- that he were and was very skeptical about the possibility of the pilots being released on that day. We told him that the talks to achieve that objective would probably be long. Some time had passed and then we told General Mladic that he would be meeting General Douin. This was at about 11.00 or 12.00 a.m. Once General Perisic had managed to persuade General Douin about the actual reality of the situation -- and I have to say that General Douin had gone back to the plane at least twice to confer with someone, probably President Chirac, because his advisors had set up a special antennae for him to be able to maintain a direct line through to Paris. And we didn't know at this time whether General Douin would be back for the talks. Nevertheless, we were happy to eventually see him back. And then some more time went by --

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I you said, at page 38, line 8: "Some time had passed and then we told General Mladic that he would be meeting General Douin. That was about 11.00 or 12.00 a.m." And was it Mladic that you told would be meeting General Douin or General Douin who you told would be meeting General Mladic?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VUKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Both.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: So General Mladic was --

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VUKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You have military men, high ranking ones, meeting like that. You have to be very specific about the time and the meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay. Well, that's what I want to be because I want to make sure that we're clear about what happened. Because, as I understand it, some period of time transpired before the two generals actually met together. When General Douin arrived at the air strip, was General Mladic present? By that I mean present in the area.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VUKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: How long a period of time, if you know, transpired between General Douin's arrival and your recognition that General Mladic was in the general area?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VUKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Two hours from the time that was set as the time the meeting and the talks would begin. I'll never forget that. Why? Because when we told General Mladic that he would now have to go to the other room in order to meet and talk with General Douin - if this is not a word that the interpreters are familiar with, can they please request further explanations - Mladic said, We were supposed to meet two hours ago; now it is me who will keep him waiting for another two hours, and then eventually I'll be the one calling the shot as to whether we would be meeting or not. Well, this -- that spelled for us was more difficult hours ahead. General Douin had now been told about the real situation, and it was up to us now to try and talk Mladic into perhaps curtailing the waiting time that he had imposed so that the two negotiators could finally meet and debate this grave problem. This was eventually the case.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: So let me understand something. From what you've told us, with the signing of the Dayton Agreement hanging in the balance, you have the initial task, and by that I mean General Perisic has the initial task, which seems to have become somewhat arduous, but the initial task of just getting these two men into the same room so that a conversation can be had; is that what you are telling us?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VUKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is precisely what I was telling you, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: How many hours of negotiation were involved before General Perisic was successful in the simple act of getting two men into the same room to discuss a matter which could dramatically affect something as minor as the Dayton Agreement? I'm just dealing with how long it took to get them into the same room, nothing more for the moment.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VUKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Between three and three and a half hours, the way I remember it.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: After the three- to three-and-a-half-hour period transpired, from what you've told us, I guess it would be General Mladic who relented and decided that he would be responsible enough to come to the room to speak with General Douin? And if my characterisation is a bit bold, I do apologise.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VUKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, you were not too bold. He managed to impose his will which was very important, bearing in mind the structure of his personality both as a human being and as a military person. Once he decided that, to meet General Douin, it was when the meeting happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: What I'd like to do at this point, if I could, is I'd like to have you go to tab 39 in your binder, which is --

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And I believe that we are going to have to be in private session for this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: May the Chamber please move into private session.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: This document, I believe --

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are in private session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: This document, I believe, has been previously admitted into evidence as 3339D. And, Mr. Thomas, I also believe it's on your XN list as 505. So between the two numbers, I believe you'll be able to grab it. I've been corrected. I'm told it's in an MFI situation perhaps. In any event ...

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, 65 ter 03339D was never used before. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay. Then I stand corrected.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I'd like you to take a look --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: In fact, we -- okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Since this is part of the Mladic diary and I've not been privy to discussions that have been had back and forth with regard to the use of the Mladic diary, I was left with the impression it has been used before. But if it hasn't been used before, that's fine. We're exactly where we should be. We're in private session, and I think all parties know which document we are referring to. If you'll excuse me for a moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Mr. Thomas, I've just been informed by Mr. Lukic that I need to obtain permission from you to use this particular document, since it's apparently on your side of the aisle, not mine, at this time. I request such permission.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: Your Honours, if what my friend is asking me is whether I agree to this going on to the Defence 65 ter list, I have no objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Thomas.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I think --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ... that's what you were asking for.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I think that the Is have been dotted and Ts crossed, at least with regard to this issue. And I thank you, Mr. Thomas.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: If you could return to the first page of this particular document, sir. And the document starts out, after listing the individuals who were present at the meeting, it says that General Perisic opened the meeting with a brief introduction, thereafter there is an entry as to what General Douin said. In that regard, it indicates that he said that I come here -- "I do not come here as an enemy, but as a negotiator. President Chirac is the commander of the OS, and I'm the chief joint GS of the OS of France." So my question to you here is: What was your understanding of General Douin's position with regard to the negotiation concerning the release of the French pilots?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VUKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Before I answer your question directly, allow me to go back to what we called perhaps fatigue. It is obvious that when I addressed the participants of the meeting, I omitted to mention General Grahovac. And I see that his name is there. And he indeed attended the meeting. I said that General Velickovic was there, but he was not there the whole time. It was quite understandable because he was commander of the air force and anti-aircraft defence, and the site where the meeting was taking place was under his command. So these discrepancies could happen, but they do not have a decisive impact. Now, back to your question, Mr. Guy-Smith. At the time, I was already more than fully informed about the way in which communications and interface were conducted and the role of persons who carried out special tasks. I understood the role of General Douin to be one that was very sensitive and that -- one that he was not very familiar with. Because he was not very knowledgeable about the region itself and the relations prevailing there, that he had just assumed the position of the chief of the joint staff, and that perhaps he had been given tasks and instructions that probably were not commensurate with the situation that he actually faced upon his arrival in Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Looking at this particular document, it indicates that General Douin asked a couple of questions, which I take it he posed to General Mladic, those being with regard to the --

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VUKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Excuse me. And the questions regarded the physical condition of the pilots?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Can we see that, please, on the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: It's the very first page, Your Honour, down at the bottom. It's pages -- it's 1 of 5 -- and it's page 2 of 5. It says --

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: It's page 1 in B/C/S and 2 in English. The questions are -- Do you see it, Your Honour? Do you have it on your screen? "Can you confirm for me on your soldierly honour ..." and it continues.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Were those questions asked -- were those questions answered by General Mladic at the time, if you know?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VUKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The questions that are mentioned here that were put by General Douin and recorded by General Mladic are exactly the questions that General Douin had put. That shows that what I previously said was correct; he thought or perhaps he had the task to return them the very same evening to Paris. Beforehand, a doctor would examine them. He expected the pilots to be somewhere nearby so that they could be handed over to him. That shows, at the same time, what a sensitive and difficult role General Douin had and the extent to which this was not the actual state of affairs.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: My question to you is: Did General Mladic answer General Douin's questions? When General Douin's asked, Are the pilots alive, What is their physical condition, did General Mladic answer those questions?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VUKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I had just intended to answer that part of the question. General Mladic did not mention the questions that were put by General Douin. Rather, he started these long remarks --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Let me interrupt you. The transcript says General Mladic did not "mention" the questions that were put by General Douin. Now, is that what you said or did you say General Mladic did not "answer" the questions? Here it says "mention the questions." The question to you is: Did he answer the questions?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
