utterances.text: [Interpretation] He did not even mention them, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Nor did he answer them?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] At that moment, he did not want to mention these questions, and his own remarks moved in a completely different direction.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay. So I take it he didn't answer the questions at that time. You may proceed, Mr. Guy-Smith.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I notice that you're nodding in response to Judge Moloto's last question, which is that he did not answer the questions at that time; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VUKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: You mentioned that he went off in a -- his own remarks moved in a completely different direction. What did he discuss?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VUKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again, bearing in mind General Mladic's personality and his structure, to put it in the briefest possible terms, he wanted to lead the game, regardless of who was involved. And he started his long remarks on the conditions under which this might happen, that the General Douin had asked for, that is. However, he did that so skillfully that on the basis of his remarks, it was hard for you to conclude that he was ready at all to meet any one of these requests.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: How long did these discussions last on the 11th of December?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VUKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, forgive me, but I cannot be very specific now. I think that the lunch had not been served actually, the lunch that had been planned. So nobody had eaten. At some point in time, the then-President of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia Lilic came to the airport, and that all of that lasted up until sometime between 11.30 p.m. and midnight on the 11th of December.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: By the conclusion --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Sorry, sir. I'm sorry to do this to you. It lasted until about 11.00 or midnight of that day having started at what time? What was the time that General Douin arrived at the meeting? Or rather, let me rephrase: After that three to three and a half hours of waiting, at what time did the meeting start?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The meeting started around 1430 hours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Gives you an idea.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: At the conclusion of the meeting on the 11th of December, I take it from what you've told us that no resolution had occurred? And by that I mean the French pilots had not been released.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VUKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let me start from the end of your question. On that day, the French pilots had not been released, but considerable progress had been made by virtue of the fact that it had been concluded that the talks would continue on the next day at a certain point in time in Mali Zvornik.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Let me stop you there.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: At this point in time, I'd like to take this particular document off the screen and move back into open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: And are you not tendering it?

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Not at this very moment. You know what, Your Honour, it might make it easier just to tender it at this moment. And that way that will be done and we don't have to go back and forth. If we could tender this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Just after I had written "not tendered."

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Sorry. As I said, I think earlier today, I'm not doing particularly well why my logistics.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: It's admitted into evidence. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours this document shall be given Exhibit D370.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And I believe that should be under seal.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Admitted under seal.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And if we could -- if we could now go into open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You said D?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit D370, admitted under seal. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are back in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you. May I request -- okay good.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: You've just told us that on the 11th of December the French pilots had not been released but considerable progress had been made by virtue of the fact that it had been concluded that talks would continue on the next day in Mali Zvornik. I'd like to pick up -- I'd like to pick up from there. Now, with regard to the talks the next day in Mali Zvornik, to your knowledge was General Perisic part of those conversations?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VUKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. On the previous day, the talks had shown that his role was a decisive one.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: When you say that "his role was a decisive one," could you please explain to us what you mean by that?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VUKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, to this day, I'm convinced that it is only General Perisic, in view of the position he held then and the way in which he operated in all of these peace efforts to observe what had been agreed upon, that he was the only person who could influence his colleague, the Chief of General Staff of the French army, in order for him to understand the situation that he was in was considerably different from what he had expected. On the other hand, he could influence General Mladic in order for him to understand that it was not a question of his vanity. I don't know whether that is the right term. It is his will that is involved. And the situation and peace in the region depended on that.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I trust that when you're talking about vanity you're not talking about the vanity of General Perisic, but, rather, the vanity of General Mladic? You're not -- you're not ascribing that particular --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I think it's clear from --

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay. I just wanted to make sure it is. General Perisic --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... is anything but a vain man; it's not something that he is.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's not what I said. It pertains to General Mladic.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Perfect. Perfect. What I'd like to do now, if we could, is if you could go to tab 22 in your binder. This is 65 ter 1090D. And I'd like you to take a look at this. And after you've examined it, if you could tell us.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VUKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have studied this document. I recognise it, and it went through my hands at the moment when it was supposed to be delivered to General Perisic.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And in that regard, I'd only like to deal with one aspect of this document which is paragraph 3. It says: "He is fully aware of General Perisic's decisive personal contribution to the positive resolution of both these cases. This also made him realise how much the VJ Chief of General Staff is committed to peace." Now, is that particular statement, that is made here by Colonel Vialatte, one that was communicated to you, independent of this particular letter?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VUKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. As for such assessments regarding General Perisic's activities, I heard them on different occasions from different foreign military attachés and other interlocutors of mine from international organisations.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: As you sit here right now, when you say "from different foreign military attachés," could you please identify any other foreign military attachés that you heard such assessments regarding General Perisic's activities from?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VUKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can say that, although, at the time, these were sensitive issues; however, I believe that today it is no secret any longer and it could not work to anyone's detriment. For instance, what the Italian military attaché said to me, a colonel whose name I cannot recall this very instant, but we called him Pino because we were very close in the contacts and the talks we had. What he said always went beyond what one could expect from an official foreign military representative. I knew how to appreciate that. Since I knew how to appreciate that, that's why he said that to me. Then Colonel Vialatte in his own way was open too. And he was not afraid of mentioning things and indicating things that he may have thought that I had not noticed, or perhaps he may have thought that these matters were not attached particular importance to in the Army of Yugoslavia. As far as I know, to my satisfaction, there is a person who testified several times before this Tribunal and that is the British military attaché Colonel Crosland, and so on and so forth. Talks with Russian military representatives were, as a rule, a bit freer, and perhaps more things were said on these occasions than otherwise would be expected; although, I was cautious when talking to these people for reasons that only I could understand and that I did not wish to share with others, and so on. Of course, the representatives of the United Nations, the United Nations office in Belgrade, they were very open and frank too. The head of that office Mr. Julian Harston was very frank. As far as I know, he held that position in Belgrade three times. Also, members of the monitoring mission were very open, the European Community Monitoring Mission that has been mentioned several times now. They increasingly understood the complexity of the problems in the Balkans, including the area of the former Yugoslavia. If that will suffice, I perhaps could end on that note.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: It does. And when you -- I just want to make sure that when --

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VUKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Allow me, please. Perhaps my answer is quite superfluous, if I did not say what I wanted to say at the very outset. It all boiled down to the following: That they made a clear distinction between the behaviour and actions of the current political leadership of the then-Federal Republic of Yugoslavia on the one hand; and on the other hand, the Army of Yugoslavia headed by General Perisic. I was grateful to them for that. But I was also surprised. Sometimes I thought that they were even exaggerating. This distinction was so important for them, and I was assured of that later as a military attaché when discussing a dramatic events. I'm not going to mention it now, but, if necessary, I could explain that as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I thank you for your answer. When you were indicating they were very open, I take it what you meant by that is their openness, amongst other things, related to the statement that I read to you from Vialatte concerning General Perisic's decisive personal contribution to the positive resolution of these cases in peace, since that was the thrust of the underlying question?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VUKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This question --

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And I would move for the admission of the last exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The document is admitted into evidence. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, this document shall be assigned Exhibit D371. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: And, Mr. Guy-Smith, would that be a convenient time?

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: It would be an excellent time, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: We'll take a break and come back at half past 12.00. Court adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Guy-Smith.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I'd like to direct your attention, now, to matters in 1997. And specifically I'd like to discuss with you, at this time, matters relating to a number of demonstrations that occurred in January of 1997. First of all, as you sit here today, do you recall there being any demonstrations in Belgrade in 1997, January?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VUKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember, Mr. Guy-Smith; however, these demonstrations started earlier, already in 1996, in the autumn of 1996, and they went into January 1997.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And when you say "these demonstrations started in the autumn of 1996," could you inform the Chamber as to the subject matter of these demonstrations?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VUKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The relationship between the opposition and the current government of Slobodan Milosevic had already been strained, and the immediate pretext were local elections. Directly, it had to do with the fact that Slobodan Milosevic did not want to recognise the result of the elections in Belgrade, since, in that case, the opposition would have taken over, would have been in government because they had won the election in Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And with regard to the participants of these demonstrations in January, can you identify, if you know, who was participating in these demonstrations?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VUKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The people took part in these demonstrations. The population of Belgrade belonging to all social structures. The demonstrations were led by the coalition that was in force then between the Democratic Party, the Serbian Renewal Movement, and some other smaller parties.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Did there --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: If I may just say something. I still have problems with my screen here. It's stuck. And it does move, but it's far behind.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Guy-Smith. You may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Did there come a time when you became involved in any discussions or planning as a member of the VJ with regard to these demonstrations?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VUKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And could you explain to us what occurred?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VUKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Since the protests at Belgrade university were very well organised and went on for a long time, students were one of the structures that took part in these negotiations. And one day the students asked that their representatives be received by the Chief of General Staff of the Army of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: At that time who was the Chief of Staff of the Army of Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VUKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do apologise for not saying what is necessary and what is generally known. The Chief of General Staff of the Army of Yugoslavia was Colonel-General Momcilo Perisic.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Were you involved in any of the decisions with regard to whether or not General Perisic would receive representatives from the student movement?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VUKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. To the extent to which General Perisic deemed this necessary.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And when you say "to the extent to which General Perisic deemed it necessary," to what extent was your involvement, if you could tell us, with General Perisic?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VUKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: One day, the so-called red telephone rang. I knew it was General Perisic. He asked me whether I had heard that the students were asking to be received by him, and I said yes. Further on, he asked me what I thought about that. I thought about it briefly and I said that in my view he should receive them. He said, It's easy for you to say, but you know how sensitive that question is. I said to him that I was fully aware of the sensitivity of the question involved but that I still believed that he should receive them. General Perisic said, All right, Vule - that's what he called me then; it has do with my last name. And then the telephone line went dead. I knew that I was not the first and only person that General Perisic would consult, but I was pleased that he had asked me. I knew that General Perisic received the students, but, of course, I was not present since it would not have been right for me to be there. Then, once again, General Perisic called me and said, See, I received them, and now tell me what do you think, should we make that public? And I said that I thought we should make that public, as was the case in some other situations. The public deserved to be informed about such things. This is what he said to me, in a friendly way, he said, There you go again. When I saw that there was a statement that had been released for the public, some people said that Milosevic had reacted in a pretty bad way and asked for the statement to be withdrawn. Again, Perisic said, Now what? See what you've got me into. Are we going withdraw the release? And I said, No way.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Let me stop you there just for a moment, if I could. You said there was a statement that had been released for the public, and what was the statement that was released for the public?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VUKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This statement for the public was something that I wasn't willing to read at all. It could have been longer or shorter, but the essence was the crucial thing, and that is that he had received them and this act in itself was so significant, even if he hadn't told them anything and even if that had not been made public. Later on, after reading the statement, I realised that part of this press release said that the army was not going to be involved in any way in that particular segment of political life, or something to that effect. I think that was the key point.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And with regard to the position taken by General Perisic that the army was not going to be involved in, as you've phrased it, "that particular segment of political life," to your knowledge were there any other state organs that had taken a different position, or were all state organs in accord with General Perisic with regard to involvement in terms of the protests that were going on?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VUKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would like to reply to your question, but please give me some poetic licence. I would like to remind you that the then-minister of the interior Mr. Milan Milutinovic, to my surprise, reacted in an unexpected fashion, in that the Ministry of the Interior informed the public what it thought about the requests posed by the international community with regard to finding a solution to the problem and requesting Mr. Milosevic to respect the will of the people expressed in the election. Later on, Mr. Milan Milutinovic was dismissed from his post as the minister of the interior. Now I know why that happened, and that was precisely the reason why he was dismissed. The only organ that acted positively was the Ministry of the Interior, and that surprised me very much, because I knew it was the Ministry of the Interior who should react in a situation where you have demonstrations because they might turn ugly. The ministry was not following this line, but, rather, they were prepared to carry out Slobodan Milosevic's order, should he give them one. I don't know anything about the reactions by other government organs.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Excuse me, if I might, I'm getting some consternation from my colleagues with regard to the position that Milan Milutinovic had at that time. Was he the minister of the interior or the minister of foreign affairs?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VUKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Milan Milutinovic was the minister of foreign affairs of the FRY at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VUKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was never minister of the interior.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Because we were getting a translation of minister of the interior here and just -- we just wanted to make sure about that. Do you -- have you ever heard the name Zoran Sokolovic.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VUKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I have.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And could you please tell us who Zoran Sokolovic is or was?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VUKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Zoran Sokolovic was the minister of the interior, whether of the Republic of Serbia -- yes, of the Republic of Serbia. He and his successor both committed suicide, and the latter was Zoran Stojiljkovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: With regard to Zoran Sokolovic -- excuse me --

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VUKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sorry. Allow me, I misspoke. Vlajko Stojiljkovic was the name.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: With regard to the gentleman I asked you about, Zoran Sokolovic, what was his position with regard to the demonstrations that were occurring? And by that I mean did he support them, was he against them, was he in favour of what was going on? Did he issue any statements with regard to them?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VUKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Zoran Sokolovic, as the minister of the interior, did not support those demonstrations. I think, although I cannot remember exactly, that the Ministry of the Interior issued statements on the issue, and that these statements, to say the least, were warnings addressed to those who participated in the demonstrations.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And with regard to these demonstrations, you've told us that General Perisic indicated that the army would not become involved in this. With regard to the Ministry of Interior, what was the relationship of the police to the Ministry of Interior?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VUKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In response to one of the questions asked of me previously, I had already indicated that in my view there were disturbed or disrupted relations between the Ministry of the Interior and the Ministry of Defence, i.e., the Yugoslav Army.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Let's stop you just there, sir. That's not the question you are being asked. The question you are being asked is the relationship between the police and the Ministry of Interior.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I can say in response to this question that the issue of these relationships were governed by specific documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: That's fine. Thank you. That's fine. That's fine. With regard to the demonstrations that were occurring, while the demonstrations were occurring, to your knowledge were there or were there not any armed police or riot police on the streets during these demonstrations?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VUKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, there were. I remember to the demonstration of the 9th of March, 1991, and with anxiety I was observing this riot police that was fully equipped to break up the demonstration, and they were acting and performing their duties in the very centre of Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: You referred us to 1991. I'm focusing us in 1997. When -- with regard to that period of time, would your answer be the same or would it be different as regards to the riot police?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VUKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would give you the same answer. These police forces, as far as I can remember, clashed with the demonstrators on the street called Terazije, which is in down-town Belgrade. And some people got injured as a result.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And when you say that the riot police were fully equipped, if you know, could you tell us what kind of equipment they were armed with at the time that they clashed with the student demonstrators?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VUKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were fully equipped in terms of how they were dressed. They had batons for physical prevention of individuals doing something, and they also had shields in front of them that they used to defend themselves against possible assault. And nearby there must have been a vehicle with water cannons that would break up the demonstrations with powerful jets of water, which is common practice. We were wondering at the time whether we had Martic's men there as well. And Martic's men were, at the time, forces that constituted a police brigade, but I don't know for sure what kind of forces those were. If necessary, Milosevic would resort to bringing them over from Knin.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Now, you indicated that after General Perisic made the statement that he made, there was some discussion as to whether or not the statement should be retracted after the directions of Slobodan Milosevic to do so. So we understand what's clearly going on at the time, when Slobodan Milosevic directed General Perisic to retract the statement, what was the result of that?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VUKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I cannot say that it's quite clear to me what you are asking me, but you have to bear in mind that already at the time the wife of Slobodan Milosevic, Mirjana Markovic, had become a very powerful personality and she said, We are not going to give up Belgrade without blood shed. We liberated Belgrade by shedding blood, and we are not going to give it up otherwise. So that was the atmosphere that prevailed, and that was the situation at the time. As far as the retraction of the statement is concerned, that was considered to be something common place. What wasn't pleasing to the eyes and ears of Slobodan Milosevic and his wife was simply going to disappear. And this is all I'm going to say on that issue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Do you know, sir, whether indeed General Perisic did withdraw the statement as a result of Slobodan Milosevic's demand that he does so?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. Now I see that I forgot to say that because I thought it was self-explanatory. No, this statement was not retracted.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Thank you for that answer. If you could go to your binder, sir, and look at tab 30, which is 65 ter 1175D. In it's English only. And if you could take a look at the -- at this document. And indicate to us when you've finished looking at the document.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VUKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I have familiarised myself with this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And are these the --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone please for the counsel.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And are these the events that you have been referring to in your testimony?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VUKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, they are. These are the events.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I would move for the admission of this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The document is admitted into evidence. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, this document shall be assigned Exhibit D372. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much. Yes, Mr. Guy-Smith.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Now, I'd like to -- for a moment, before the document goes off the screen, I'd like to go to -- I believe it's the third page. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And on the third page there's an article in which there is a quote which is - one, two, three, four, five - six paragraphs down that says: "'Serbia will explode after January 9th.' Vasiljevic warned." Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VUKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Can you tell us, if you know, to what extent the position that General Perisic took that the army would not intervene in this political, and if I might be so bold as to say, social strife, had on the concerns that Serbia itself would explode? And if my question is ambiguous, put in other terms: Was General Perisic's meeting with the students and statement salutary in terms of keeping violence to a minimum, if not non-existent, within -- with regard to these demonstrations?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VUKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the time, I did not notice this statement made by this young man by the name of Vasiljevic, so I still don't understand what this short sentence might refer to, whether he meant that the demonstrators would radicalise their protests or whether Serbia would explode in a democratic sense, that is to say, that the people would eventually realise that Slobodan Milosevic was not omnipotent and that his position was sufficiently endangered, that other measures could be taken that would direct Serbia onto the road of democracy. At this point, I'm not able to make the distinction.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Well, with that answer -- with that answer in mind, in terms of whether the protests would be further radicalised or whether Serbia would explode in a democratic sense, I'd like to discuss with you something that we talked about at the very beginning of your testimony which is the political party that you alluded to that both you and General Perisic were members of, the Movement For Democratic Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And if we could in that regard have up on the screen 65 ter 1192D, which would be tab 32 in your binder.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Are you familiar with this document?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VUKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I am.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I would move its admission.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The document is admitted into evidence. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, this document shall be assigned Exhibit D373. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Now, to put this into perspective, at the time that this political party was formed, was General Perisic still the Chief of Staff of the army of the VJ?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VUKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, he wasn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And could you tell us, if you know, when General Perisic ceased being Chief of Staff of the VJ army?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VUKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe that you're not expecting me to tell you the exact date, but he was dismissed from the position of the Chief of General Staff in early November 1998. Before that, he did avert [as interpreted] a speech in his native town of Gornji Milanovac, which was actually the cause for his dismissal.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And what was the subject matter of that speech, sir?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VUKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Very briefly, the essence was that no country must be in conflict with the whole world. That was a very serious condemnation of the policies pursued at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I'd like to turn your attention now to what is tab 34 in your binder, which is 65 ter 1056D. I ask you to take a look at that document, if you would, please.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VUKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm familiar with this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And when you say you are familiar with this document, were you aware of the press conference that he held that caused criminal charges to be brought against him?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VUKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Do you know what the ultimate outcome was with regard to this particular prosecution against, at that time it would be Mr. Perisic, formerly General Perisic?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VUKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The outcome was the same as in the proceedings against me. On the 5th of October, Milosevic's regime was overthrown after peaceful demonstrations in Belgrade. The new people in power didn't quite know how to handle the situation concerning this judgement passed by Milosevic's regime.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Just a second, Mr. Vuksic. You said that Milosevic's regime was overthrown on the 5th of October, of which year?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 1999, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay. And then you also say that people who came into the new government did not know how to handle this judgement passed by the Milosevic regime. Now, this is not a judgement that we see on the screen, this is a charge sheet. This is a charge -- or is it a judgement?

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: No, Your Honour, you're absolutely --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: It's Criminal charges --

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: No, you're absolutely -- you're absolutely correct; they are criminal charges.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: So the question is whether did the new government proceed with the charges against Mr. Perisic, or what did they do with this charge sheet?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I thank you for this question. General Perisic was punished by having his rank removed, reserve colonel general. He now no longer held that rank and was left a man without a past. His pension payments were also terminated. He was left without any means of sustenance. All of this was entirely unlawful, arbitrary, and simply a result of a person's political will. When I said the new authorities or the new people in power had trouble handling the situation, as all of you lawyers here know, the most difficult task for a lawyer is to deal with a case that is not founded on any legal basis, but, rather, is a result of tyranny and wanton ambition on the part of certain individuals. You have to make a ruling or a decision in that case that is baseless in terms of law simply because the law offers no foundation for dealing with a case that is in itself irregular. This is the best I can say it, and I certainly hope that your understanding of matters such as this one is better than mine.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: If I might, Mr. Vuksic, in response to the question of Judge Moloto, when he asked you in what year the Milosevic regime was overthrown, the transcript indicates 1999 as the year in which Milosevic's regime was overthrown. Is that correct; was it 1999?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN VUKSIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I do apologise. This is another thing that we might call wear and tear. It was, as a matter of fact, on the 5th of October, and the year was 2000. I am sorry, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: That's fine, Mr. Vuksic. We have ten minutes to go, and you will have a good -- some rest.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Actually, I wanted to thank Mr. Vuksic for his time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Guy-Smith. Mr. Thomas?

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: I do have some cross-examination, Your Honours, but I wonder if we can leave that for tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay. Mr. Vuksic, you can say thank you to Mr. Thomas. He recognises the fact that the wear and tear is taking its toll, so he is giving you an extra ten minutes of rest. We will break at this time. We'll come back tomorrow in the same court at 9.00 in the morning. And you are still reminded not to discuss the case with anybody until you are excused from further testifying. Court adjourned.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Excuse me, Your Honour, right before we adjourn, there is a matter the I think requires our brief attention. It does not require the presence of Mr. Vuksic; he can stay or he can go. But we do need to alert the Chamber to some developments that have occurred in terms of future planning that I think may be of some importance to us all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay. Mr. Vuksic, you are excused, if you want to leave. If you don't, you can stay there. What's now going to be discussed is just how we run the case.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And if we could go into private session, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: May the Chamber please move into private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Friday, the 25th day of June, 2010, at 9.00 a.m. 23 24 25
